  <section class="tour-section">

    <h2>About This Florida Food Forest</h2>

    <p>
      A food forest does not need to occupy several acres to contain remarkable
      diversity. KC’s garden demonstrates how a relatively small residential
      property can become a densely layered edible landscape.
    </p>

    <p>
      Rather than treating each fruit tree as an isolated specimen surrounded
      by open space, the garden uses close planting, vertical layers, and nearly
      every available growing area. The result is a living collection in which
      tropical fruit trees, shrubs, vines, and smaller edible plants grow
      together throughout the property.
    </p>

    <p>
      During this tour, we explore the plants, layout, and growing decisions
      that allow KC to maintain such an extensive collection in a limited area.
      The garden offers ideas for anyone interested in increasing diversity
      without owning a large farm or homestead.
    </p>

  </section>


  <section class="tour-section">

    <h2>What You’ll Learn</h2>

    <div class="learn-grid">

      <div class="learn-item">
        How a small residential property can hold an extensive edible collection
      </div>

      <div class="learn-item">
        How high-density planting differs from a conventional orchard layout
      </div>

      <div class="learn-item">
        How multiple vertical layers make better use of limited garden space
      </div>

      <div class="learn-item">
        Why plant placement becomes especially important in a crowded food forest
      </div>

      <div class="learn-item">
        How tropical fruit diversity can become the central theme of a home landscape
      </div>

      <div class="learn-item">
        Ideas that can be adapted to smaller backyards and urban properties
      </div>

    </div>

  </section>


  <section class="tour-section">

    <h2>What Makes This Garden Abundant?</h2>

    <p>
      The defining feature of this food forest is its density. Instead of
      relying on a few large trees separated by open lawn, the garden fits many
      edible species into a compact residential landscape.
    </p>

    <p>
      The abundance comes not only from the number of plants, but from the way
      the available space is used. Taller trees create an upper layer, smaller
      fruit trees and shrubs occupy the middle, while vines, herbs, and other
      edible plants fill additional niches.
    </p>

    <p>
      KC’s garden shows that abundance can mean diversity, experimentation, and
      the ability to step outside and encounter something edible almost
      everywhere you look.
    </p>

  </section>

      <li>
